conceptPrimer.heading: Equilibrium Is a Standoff, Not a Stoppage
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Picture two opposite reactions running at the same speed: products form exactly as fast as they break back down, so concentrations freeze while molecules keep colliding — dynamic, never dead. The balance point is measured by an equilibrium constant: for $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$, $K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ (products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient). The value of $K$ depends ONLY on temperature — a catalyst, a pressure change or a concentration change shifts the position of the balance but never the constant itself. Reverse the equation and $K$ inverts ($\frac{1}{K}$); multiply the equation by $n$ and $K$ is raised to the power $n$; and for gas reactions $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ counts gaseous moles, products minus reactants.

conceptPrimer.heading: Le Chatelier in One Breath
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Disturb a balanced reaction and it shifts so as to cancel the disturbance: add a reactant and the forward direction wins; squeeze a gas mixture and it slides toward the side with fewer gas moles; heat an exothermic reaction and it shifts backward, because heat behaves like a product. For electrolytes the same law becomes the common-ion effect: a salt that shares an ion with a weak acid or base suppresses its ionization. Ostwald's dilution law says it precisely — $K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \approx C\alpha^2$ for weak electrolytes — so dilution RAISES the degree of ionization $\alpha$ while the constant $K_a$ stays put at a given temperature.

conceptPrimer.heading: $K_{sp}$ — the Give-Up Point of a Salt
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: For a sparingly soluble salt $A_xB_y \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}$, the solubility product is $K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x[B^{x-}]^y$, written with saturated-solution (equilibrium) concentrations. Everything reduces to one comparison between the ionic product $Q$ (computed from whatever concentrations actually exist right now) and $K_{sp}$: $Q < K_{sp}$ means unsaturated and more can dissolve; $Q = K_{sp}$ means saturated, exactly at the edge; $Q > K_{sp}$ means a precipitate forms until $Q$ falls back to $K_{sp}$. That single comparison answers every 'will it precipitate?' question, and common ions or pH changes push solubility down through the same Le Chatelier logic.

memoryHooks: $K$ changes only with temperature — everything else merely shifts the position, never the constant.
Reverse the equation → $K$ flips to $\frac{1}{K}$; multiply the equation by $n$ → $K$ becomes $K^n$.
$K_p = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n}$ — count only GAS moles, products minus reactants.
$pH + pOH = 14$ at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, and $K_a \cdot K_b = K_w$ for any conjugate pair.
Buffer recipe: weak partner + its salt; when $[\text{salt}] = [\text{acid}]$, $pH = pK_a$ exactly.
Lower $pK_a$ = stronger acid; and $Q > K_{sp}$ means 'precipitate now'.
commonMistakes: Using the strong-acid shortcut on weak acids: for $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, $[\text{H}^+] \neq C$ — go through $K_a$ and $\alpha$ (Ostwald) or you will grossly overstate $[\text{H}^+]$.
Confusing the degree of ionization $\alpha$ with the ionization constant $K_a$: dilution raises $\alpha$ but $K_a$ stays fixed at a given temperature.
Plugging concentrations into $K$ before the ICE table has reached its equilibrium row — only equilibrium values belong in the constant.
Writing $K_p = K_c(RT)^{+\Delta n}$ blindly — the SIGN of $\Delta n$ decides whether $K_p$ comes out larger or smaller than $K_c$.
Comparing $Q$ with $K_{sp}$ using initial and equilibrium concentrations mixed together — both quantities must be computed on the same basis (for mixing questions, the diluted concentrations).
examChecklist: Classify first: strong or weak electrolyte? It decides whether $[\text{H}^+]$ comes from $C$ directly or from $K_a$ and $\alpha$.
Write the balanced equation and count $\Delta n$ (gas moles only) before touching $K_p$ or $K_c$.
Set up the ICE table with a single unknown $x$ and keep every entry in mol/L.
At $25^{\circ}\text{C}$: $K_w = 10^{-14}$, $pH + pOH = 14$, neutral $pH = 7$ — and remember this trio is temperature-bound.
Buffer questions: identify the weak partner and its salt, then apply Henderson–Hasselbalch directly.
Conjugate pairs: pick the missing constant via $K_a \cdot K_b = K_w$, never guess both.
Precipitation questions: compute $Q$ from the MIXED (diluted) concentrations, then compare against $K_{sp}$.
